Note to Self: Does TuneJury already cover generator-identity exploitation?

GPT 6 Ultra gives me the following table, after being prompted something along the lines of “pinpoint paragraphs where the paper TuneJury covers my question”:

Experiment What it establishes
Appendix D, p.22: generator-conditioned directional errors The evaluator systematically favors or disfavors outputs associated with particular generators.
Appendix D, pp.22–23: generator-specific score corrections Generator metadata helps correct prediction errors, even with the original evaluator frozen.
Appendix I, p.31: identical MIDI rendered using different soundfonts Scores and rankings depend on rendering, while symbolic composition stays fixed.

A closer look of the paper reveals that this table is not an accurate summary of what has already been established.

First row

Instead of the sweeping statement of “systematically favors or disfavors outputs associated with particular generators”, the paper only establishes the following (regarding the first row of the table above):

Comparisons considered Evaluator’s disagreement
Humans choose the competitor over ACE-Step TuneJury chooses ACE-Step in 73.6% of these comparisons.
Humans choose MusicGen-medium over its competitor TuneJury chooses the competitor in 83.8% of these comparisons.

Let decipher what this finding does and doesn’t tell us. First note that \[ P(\text{error}) = P(\text{human pick competitor})\times0.736 + P(\text{human pick ACE-step})\times P(\text{evaluator pick competitor} \mid \dots). \] How does this relate to generator-identity exploitation? Evaluators may have learned to favor ACE-step’s distinctive sound characteristics even when these are unrelated to musical quality. Without the other three quantities (two are independent), however, this remains speculative. If ACE-step is highly competitive and humans rarely prefer its competitors, the reported 73.6% human-disagreement rate may be less alarming than it initially appears.

Knowing the other three quantities on the right-hand side could provide much more insight regarding generator-identity exploitation. For example, if humans usually prefer ACE-step, but evaluators rarely pick competitors even when humans prefer them, this would be consistent with evaluators relying on ACE-step’s overall strength as a shortcut. It would support, though not establish, the hypothesis of generator-identity exploitation.

Second Row

The TuneJury paper uses a calibration set to learn generator-specific offsets. To do so, they model human-preference using the B-T model \[ \operatorname{logit}P(a\succ b) =r(a)-r(b)-\beta_{g(a)}+\beta_{g(b)}, \] where \(\beta_{g(a)}\) denotes the offset coefficient for the genrator of clip \(a\). Those offsets are trained during the calibration phrase while keeping the reward model \(r\) frozen. The use of generator-specific offset indicates that the authors intend to exploit generator identity.

The greatest problem I see with this approach is its inability to adapt to unseen generators: we do not have a way to learn the offset for a new generator \(g_{\mathrm{new}}\) that is not in the calibration set.

Is generator-identity exploitation not a concern for TuneJury?

Here’s the application of TuneJury’s evaluator, as listed by the paper:

Application What they do What changes
Best-of-\(N\) selection Generate \(N\) clips from one generator for the same prompt; keep the clip with the highest TuneJury score. The selected output; the generator stays frozen.
Inference-time optimization Adjust the initial noise latents through gradient ascent to produce a higher-scoring clip. The sampling input; the generator stays frozen.
Generator fine-tuning Generate clips, retain the highest-scoring 10%, and fine-tune the generator on those clips. The generator’s weights.

Let’s also examine the entirety of the training data for TuneJury:

Training source Training pairs Pairing
AIME 12,480 Different generators, including generated-versus-real comparisons.
MusicPrefs 2,012 Different generators. I checked the released metadata: all 2,515 source pairs are cross-generator.
Music Arena 571 Outputs from two different generators for a user’s prompt.
SongEval 2,491 Random song pairs with sufficiently different human ratings; their code imposes no generator restriction.

Note that at least 85.8% of the training pairs are cross-generator. If generator-identity exploitation is a real phenomena, then the “effective training-pairs” can be much smaller than what initially appeared. This matters for best-of-\(N\) question, as requires automatic evaluation of samples coming from the same generator.

What’s Next

How we evaluate generator-identity exploitation: we ask LLM to generate 100 pairs of counterpoint composition consisting of X bars. We use the prompt “XXX” to ensure that one clip is good, while the other clip violates a composition rule for counterpoint. We consistently use soundfont A for the better clip and soundfont B for the other clip. Those soundfont should differ substantially in their sound profile, and a classifier using their audio embeddings should achieve high accuracy for generator classification.

For testing, we would then flip the soundfont of the better and worse compositions. If the evalutor also swaps their preference, then we know the evaluator is exploiting the sound profile.
